entries.title: Spotify More Than Doubled Monthly Code Changes as AI Accelerated Development
entries.summary: Spotify reports that AI-assisted development more than doubled monthly merged changes, prompting a review of quality and reliability controls across its engineering organization. The company describes changes to testing, observability, rollback capacity, workload prioritization, and automated maintenance as it adapts to higher software change volume. By Leela Kumili
entries.content:
Spotify has expanded its use of AI-assisted development, more than doubling monthly merged changes from approximately 8,100 to 17,000 year over year in August. The company is adapting its quality and reliability controls to handle the higher volume of software changes across its production systems.

Spotify operates nearly 3,000 production services supporting 777 million monthly active users, around 100 million concurrent clients, and 11 to 12 million backend requests per second. Its review identified issues involving content processing, fleet changes, compute capacity, and mobile application quality. The company has responded with changes to monitoring, testing, rollout safeguards, rollback capacity, capacity planning, and quality measurement.

One incident involved Spotify's content processing pipeline, which handles more than 500,000 new songs, videos, podcasts, and audiobooks each day. On June 24, a scheduled batch workload competed with new episodes, a quality improvement increased processing requirements, and a scheduling bug reduced throughput by about 10%. Episodes that normally appeared within minutes were delayed for hours. Spotify subsequently added end-to-end monitoring, fixed the scheduler, moved batch jobs to lower priority, reworked workload prioritization, and increased capacity.

Fleet automation created a different challenge. Spotify's Fleet Management system has merged more than 2.5 million automated maintenance pull requests, with most automatically merged after safety checks. The company later added Honk, a background coding agent that runs Claude using the Agent SDK in Kubernetes pods. Fleetshift handles target selection, scheduling, and progress tracking, while Honk performs code modifications and can run builds in CI. Spotify reports that a recent Java migration across its backend services took three days.

An automated dependency upgrade nevertheless passed existing checks and failed in production, according to Spotify. The company is strengthening safeguards, expanding rollback capacity, and scheduling automated changes during owning teams' working hours.

Amit Jha, a software engineer at JumpCloud, in a LinkedIn post discussing Spotify's findings, said:

More changes meant greater pressure on testing, review and observability.

Alex Beck similarly focused on the verification challenge in a LinkedIn post,

Writing code got easier. The hard part now is making sure the work is actually good before it goes live.

The findings provide context for Google's 2025 DORA research, which found that AI adoption was associated with higher software delivery throughput and product performance, while also reporting a negative relationship with delivery stability. The research identified automated testing, version control, and fast feedback loops as practices relevant to managing software delivery as AI adoption increases.

Spotify combines Fleet Management for standardized maintenance with Honk for complex code changes, while Fleetshift handles orchestration and CI provides validation. Quality and optimization work rose from 27% to 31% of merged changes, while maintenance and configuration fell from 31% to 25%. Spotify reports no corresponding increase in rework, although pull request size and code complexity are rising. Its incident review found no material direct contribution from AI-authored code, but change volume had outpaced some verification controls.

entries.title: Article: When Should You Use Liquid Clustering? Benchmarking Lakehouse Layout Strategies
entries.summary: Physical data layout is one of the most consequential decisions in lakehouse engineering. The author compares Liquid Clustering, ZOrdering, and partitioning across four workload types on Delta Lake, uncovering two undocumented failure modes that likely affect production systems today and offering a decision framework for choosing the right layout strategy. By Kushal Kumar Vishwakarma
entries.content:
Key Takeaways

  • No single storage layout is universally optimal for lakehouse analytics: The right choice is workload-dependent, because using Liquid Clustering, ZOrder, or Partitioning incorrectly can materially impact cost and latency.
  • ZOrder has a hidden failure mode. When a date column appears as a secondary or tertiary clustering key, time range queries perform significantly worse than on a simple date-partitioned table.
  • Bytes scanned is a misleading performance proxy. Liquid Clustering delivers the lowest latency on point lookups despite scanning more raw data than ZOrder.
  • Liquid Clustering should be the default for any team whose query patterns are diverse or evolving and outperforms ZOrder on most workloads while eliminating the operational burden of manual OPTIMIZE jobs and periodic full table rewrites.
  • Before finalizing any layout strategy, ask yourself: ”Do my top queries consistently filter on the same two or three columns? If the answer is yes, ZOrder those columns. Otherwise, choose Liquid Clustering.

Introduction

No single storage layout is universally optimal for lakehouse analytical systems. Across four workload types benchmarked on Delta Lake, Liquid Clustering delivers the lowest latency for point lookups, time-range aggregations, and large aggregations. Liquid Clustering should be the default for teams whose query patterns are diverse or evolving. ZOrdering performed better only for stable, highly selective multicolumn predicate workloads where the filter columns precisely match the clustering key.



Partitioning, ZOrdering, and Liquid Clustering each take a fundamentally different approach to organizing data on disk; understanding the tradeoffs is key to choosing the right one for your workload. Two of my findings stand out because they run counter to how these layouts are usually described and because they are the kind of thing that could be silently degrading a production system right now,

ZOrder’s Hidden Failure Mode on Date Ranges

When a date column sits as a secondary or tertiary key in a ZOrder clustering expression, time-range queries perform significantly worse than a simple date-partitioned table, seventy-eight percent slower in this benchmark. Sequential date values are dispersed across files, destroying the range-scan efficiency that partitioning provides for free. If your team ZOrdered on multiple columns and date is not the first key, this is almost certainly affecting your time-range query performance.

Liquid Clustering’s Precision Gap on Multicolumn Filters

When a query predicate precisely matches a stable set of filter columns, ZOrder’s file pruning is close to optimal and Liquid Clustering can be nearly five times slower while scanning ten times more data. Liquid Clustering’s broader locality optimization trades deterministic pruning for workload flexibility. That trade-off becomes a liability exactly when queries are narrow and predictable.

These results matter because physical data layout is one of the most consequential and least discussed decisions in lakehouse engineering while the trade-offs between partitioning, ZOrdering, and Liquid Clustering are usually described conceptually rather than measured.

Most published comparisons either come from Databricks itself or reason about the trade-offs from first principles without measuring actual query behavior. The questions behind this benchmark were shaped directly by production challenges I encountered while architecting Delta Lake platforms at TCS UK (civil aerospace) and IBM (Shell Maritime), where layout decisions have direct implications for pipeline SLA compliance and cloud compute cost.

My practical recommendation, before you commit to a layout strategy, is to run your top three query patterns against all three configurations, partitioned, ZOrdered, and Liquid Clustered, on a representative sample of your own data. The results below, from a controlled benchmark comparing all three layout strategies across four analytical workload types on a fifty-million-record dataset using real Databricks query profiles, may surprise you as much as they surprised me.

What This Means in Practice

Taken together, the results map out a clear decision framework based on workload type:

Workload TypeBest LayoutWhy
Point LookupLiquid ClusteringSuperior intra-file locality reduces seek overhead
TimeRange AggregationLiquid ClusteringSequential locality outperforms ZOrder's dispersed date values
MultiColumn Selective FilterZOrderPrecise file pruning 10x less data scanned
Large AggregationLiquid ClusteringHilbert curve locality wins for full scan workloads

Perhaps the single most actionable insight in this article is a deceptively simple diagnostic question that practitioners should ask before committing to any layout strategy: do my top queries consistently filter on the same two to three columns? The answer to this question alone can determine whether composite partitioning will yield meaningful gains or introduce unnecessary complexity.

If the answer is yes and those columns are known and stable, use ZOrder on exactly those columns to ensure the most selective column is listed first. If the answer is no, or if query patterns are likely to evolve, use Liquid Clustering as the default. Liquid Clustering wins on three out of four workload types and removes the operational overhead of manual OPTIMIZE scheduling. A decision helper written in Python is available on GitHub.

The sections below lay out the methodology, results, and analysis behind these recommendations, the how and why, for readers who want to verify the findings before applying them.

Experiment Setup

Below are the dataset, layout configuration, workloads, and results from the analysis.

Dataset

A synthetic transactional dataset of fifty million records was generated to simulate a retail purchase environment, with the following schema:

customer_id   INT         uniform distribution, range 12,000,000
txn_date      DATE        spanning 20192023
region        STRING      categorical: EU, US, APAC, LATAM (skewed toward EU/US)
amount        FLOAT       rightskewed, simulating highvalue outliers
product_cat   STRING      categorical, 12 categories

The mix of uniform and skewed distributions was deliberate, with parameters calibrated against empirically observed access-frequency patterns in production traces. Specifically, skew parameters such as Zipf α = 1.2 for customer segments and an 80/20 partition hot-spot split were chosen to match the distribution of query volume seen in real workloads. These values were not selected arbitrarily but derived from production telemetry, where the top twenty percent of customer segments consistently account for approximately eighty percent of query traffic, ensuring the synthetic dataset reflects real-world hot partitions and demand skew.

Layout Configuration

Partitioned table
df.write.format('delta').partitionBy('txn_date').saveAsTable('lc_partitioned')

 ZOrdered table
spark.sql('OPTIMIZE lc_zorder ZORDER BY (customer_id, region, txn_date)')

 Liquid Clustered table
spark.sql('''
  CREATE TABLE lc_liquid
  CLUSTER BY (customer_id, region, txn_date)
  AS SELECT * FROM source_data
''')

Workloads

All the queries can be found on GitHub.

Results

W1: Point Lookup

Liquid Clustering achieved the lowest latency at 1.003 seconds, forty-nine percent faster than the partitioned baseline, despite scanning more raw data than ZOrder. This is the first counterintuitive result, which produced better performance from reading more bytes. The explanation is intra-file sequential locality. Liquid Clustering's Hilbert curve organization colocates related customer_id values within files more effectively, reducing disk seek overhead and increasing scan throughput. ZOrder reduces bytes read through file pruning, but the overhead of accessing more files offsets this advantage.

ZOrder1.437s369.09 MB50% less data, slower
Liquid Clustering1.003s ✓784.86 MBBest latency

W2: TimeRange Aggregation

Liquid Clustering again achieved the lowest latency at 659 milliseconds. ZOrder's underperformed relative to the partitioned baseline: ZOrder took 1.845 seconds versus partitioning's 1.038 seconds, seventy-eight percent slower. The ZOrder clustering key was (

Figure 1a. Range aggregation, partitioned table. Source here.

Figure 1b. Range aggregation, ZOrdered table. Source here.

Figure 1c. Range aggregation, Liquid Clustered table. Source here.

W3: MultiColumn Selective Filter

This workload produced the sharpest reversal. ZOrder achieved 615 milliseconds and read only 59.03 megabytes. Liquid Clustering took 2.967 seconds and read 639.95 megabytes, nearly five times slower and scanning ten times more data. When the query predicate precisely matches the ZOrder clustering key combination, ZOrder's file pruning is near optimal. Liquid Clustering's broader locality optimization, designed for workload diversity, becomes a liability here, because it cannot achieve the same level of precise file elimination unlike ZOrder, which locks onto a fixed column order to eliminate files precisely, Liquid Clustering trades that precision for flexibility and on this workload, that tradeoff costs it. If your workload is dominated by stable, highly selective multicolumn filters on known columns, ZOrder is still the right choice.

Figure 2c. Multicolumn filter Liquid Clustered table. Source here.

W4: Large Aggregation

For a full dataset SUM aggregation grouped by region (using the same query as W2 but run without predicate filtering across the entire dataset to clarify the benchmark numbers), Liquid Clustering again achieved the lowest latency (659 milliseconds) with ZOrder the slowest (1.845 seconds). For full scan workloads file pruning provides no benefit; the determinant of performance shifts to intra-file read efficiency and task scheduling, both of which favor Liquid Clustering's Hilbert curve locality.

Liquid Clustering659ms ✓449.19 MBBest latency

Discussion

The same two mechanisms explain the results across all four workloads: file-pruning efficiency, how much data a layout avoids reading, and intra-file locality, how efficiently the read data is scanned. ZOrder and partitioning compete primarily on pruning. Liquid Clustering wins primarily on locality, via its Hilbert curve organization, even when it reads more bytes than ZOrder. Where a query precisely matches a stable clustering key, pruning dominates and ZOrder wins (W3). Where it doesn’t, or a full scan is unavoidable, locality dominates and Liquid Clustering wins (W1, W2, W4). The ZOrder date-range failure mode (W2) is the same pruning-versus-locality trade-off viewed from the other side. Making date a tertiary key sacrifices the sequential locality that a date partition gives away for free, without buying back enough pruning benefit to compensate.

Caveats

These benchmarks use a synthetic dataset to ensure reproducibility and avoid client data exposure. Real production datasets carry additional complexity, schema drift, access pattern seasonality, and domain-specific skew that may shift the relative performance of each layout. The findings presented here should be treated as a directional guide and validated against your own workload profile before making irreversible schema decisions.

Additionally, I did not measure the write amplification cost of the I/O and the compute overhead of maintaining each layout as new data arrives. Liquid Clustering's incremental approach has a lower write time cost than ZOrder's periodic full table rewrites, but this was not experimentally measured and warrants separate investigation.

Conclusion

No single storage layout is universally optimal for lakehouse analytical systems. Liquid Clustering outperforms on latency for point lookups, range scans, and large aggregations, and should be the default for teams with diverse or evolving workloads. ZOrdering performs better for stable, highly selective multicolumn predicate workloads where the filter columns precisely match the clustering key.

The two most practically significant findings, ZOrder's degradation on range scans when date is a secondary key, and Liquid Clustering's five times latency penalty on precise multicolumn filters, are failure modes that are not documented and are likely affecting production systems today.

Run your top three query patterns against all three layout configurations on a representative data sample. The results may surprise you.

entries.title: Podcast: What Does It Really Mean To Program With AI: A Conversation with Joy Ebertz
entries.summary: In this podcast, Michael Stiefel spoke to Joy Ebertz about how the use of artificial intelligence is changing the way architects and developers do their jobs. Focusing on the long term success of the business is one of the most neglected tasks of an architect. This task becomes particularly important as the nature of artificial intelligence changes the landscape of software development. By Joy Ebe
entries.content:
In this podcast, Michael Stiefel spoke to Joy Ebertz about how the use of artificial intelligence is changing the way architects and developers do their jobs. Focusing on the long term success of the business is one of the most neglected tasks of an architect. This task becomes particularly important as the nature of artificial intelligence changes the landscape of software development. Architects must be especially aware of requirements and their inherent ambiguity. More than ever, they must be expert at explaining technology to the business people, and the business to the technology people. On the flip side, goals must be clearly explained to AI agents, and tests must be unambiguously written. Industry practice is uncertain on how to incorporate changes due to bug reports or new requirements. Should it be done incrementally, or should the module’s or application’s code base be regenerated? This is especially challenging in existing systems, especially old ones where nobody knows what the real requirements were. Unambiguous requirements definition may turn out to be the gating factor in AI driven software development because code reviews seem not to be effective, and verification of the AI work is a great burden.

The conversation then shifted to talk about the future of software developers. The industry needs to find a way to use AI so that human understanding of how software systems work does not atrophy. The flexibility that AI coding gives you reinforces the idea that constraints, and the recognition of the assumptions you are making, are critical concepts on which future developers need to focus. If you look at how AI is actually used, it seems to boil down to two use cases - vibe coding for things that do not have to be perfect such as many internal tools, and essential systems where you specify to the AI, and validate the results very carefully. In the latter scenario, you are effectively pair programming with the AI. Here those constraints and assumptions must be understood. In addition, the industry has not figured out a way to train future software engineers since AI is doing the tasks on which junior engineers were traditionally trained.

Key Takeaways

  • One of the important, often neglected parts of an architect’s job is to focus on the long term implications of technical decisions that might make or break a business’ survival.
  • It is still not certain whether AI software development generally lends itself more naturally to microservices or monoliths.
  • What is meant by coding with artificial intelligence has a wide range of meaning. It ranges from vibe coding, developing internal tools, treating the AI as a closely supervised pair programmer, to being similar to a constrained senior developer.
  • As artificial intelligence takes on more of the coding workload, precise requirements and comprehensive tests in order to remove ambiguity becomes critical.
  • Industry has not yet figured out how to train junior engineers as AI coding now does much of the work on which they were trained.

Subscribe on:

Transcript

Michael Stiefel: Welcome to The Architect's Podcast where we discuss what it means to be an architect and how architects actually do their job. Today's guest is Joy Ebertz, who is a principal software engineer at Imprint where she is currently trying to detangle their configuration. She's primarily a backend focused developer with extensive experience in microservice architecture, authorization frameworks, creating REST API standards, feature flagging, and more.

Prior to Imprint, she worked at Harness, Split, and Box in staff plus roles. In addition to designing software and writing a lot of code with the help of AI, she also maintains a blog with both career and technical topics. In her free time, she does a lot of traveling, reading, and running ridiculously long distances, mostly on trails.

It's great to have you here on the podcast. And I'd like to start out by asking you, were you trained as an architect? How did you become an architect?

What is an Architect? [01:09]

Joy Ebertz: Yes. Well, thanks for having me, first of all. I guess like most career paths, it was a bit meandering. I mean, if you had asked me pretty soon out of college, "Where do you want to go eventually?" I probably would've said something like architect. I thought something like that was pretty cool. I was generally drawn to that. But then over time, I tried a few different things.

When I was at Box, I got pushed into management at one point. I lasted about a year and a half and decided I absolutely hated it. So that was the end of that career progression. I moved back to the IC track. And from there, it wasn't quite ... We didn't have a role called architect at Box, but over time, as I got more senior and started picking up more responsibilities, I tended to gravitate towards the more overarching type roles, the roles that looked into a lot of different spaces and how things fit together, how things generally worked.

And then at some point we started a project, actually we started this project five times, but on one of the iterations, we were trying to break our monolith into microservices. And so as a part of that, we spun up a small team of individuals working on doing sort of a domain-driven design exploration of the entire space. And I was lucky enough to be chosen as one of the people on that team, which caused me to learn a lot about some of the more theoretical side of architecture and dig in and really think about how code fits together. And from there, I would say I just sort of tended in that direction. And to be honest, I've never had an official architect title, but if you ask me to place myself, that's generally where I would place myself in my roles.

Michael Stiefel: Well, a lot of people who function as architects don't have that title. In fact, if you remember, there was a time in a certain phase of Agile where they said, "We're not going to have any architects". And the idea was that architecture would somehow magically emerge and everybody would be an architect. And to my way of thinking, that always doesn't work because if no one has responsibility for it, it usually doesn't get done. And I don't know if that's your experience.

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Michael Stiefel: The way I like to think about architecture, and tell me whether you disagree with that, is that the architect is responsible for those things that cannot be written in a use case. The ilities, the security, scalability, the whole user experience. I'm not talking about the user interface, but the user experience. And that really is where the architect role shines.

Joy Ebertz: I would say some of that, but also thinking long-term. I feel like sometimes some of the things you mentioned, the team might think about anyway because they happen to be in the RFC template or what have you. But I've also seen a lot of times people will think a little bit too small, either in terms of timeline or in terms of only thinking about their team or what have you. And part of where I see the architect shine is pulling in those, "Where are we going next and how does this fit with that?" as well as, "This other team is doing this thing, how does your thing work well with that?" And kind of pulling the big picture into what's actually being built.

Michael Stiefel: And part of that, as I remember from your QCon talk, I mean, you were talking at the time about technical debt, but the technical debt is just an example of this. You have to trade off, do we sacrifice too much for the long term? How much does it really matter? What's the business case for doing that?

So it's really, from what you're saying, it's not only thinking in the long term in terms of technical things, but in terms of understanding the business and explaining that to the business people as well.

Joy Ebertz: Correct. Yes. I mean, you could build something absolutely technically perfect that's going to last a hundred billion customers, whatever, but if your business doesn't survive to next month, it doesn't matter.

Michael Stiefel: Right. I think that's a valid point. What you're referring to is what Gregor Hohpe likes to talk about, the elevator architect, where he has to go from the boardroom to the boiler room. In other words, you have to be able to talk to the technical people and explain to them the business goals, and you have to explain to the business people what the technical goals are.

Joy Ebertz: Yes, exactly.

Monoliths or Microservices When Coding With AI [05:33]

Michael Stiefel: Which leads me into the first thing I'm curious about is you've talked about monoliths and you have an extensive background in microservices. There seems to be a tendency today that people are pushing back and going towards monoliths. And to me, this sort of conflicts with the use of AI to code because I think AI thinks it works better with microservices where you can see what the AI code generator does; you have bounding boxes around it. As opposed to if you have a monolith, it becomes much harder to use AI.

Joy Ebertz: Yes, that's an interesting point. Yes, I guess over the years I've seen the trend from monolith to microservices and then back to monolith. And honestly, personally, I can see good arguments in both directions. But what's fascinating is where I am currently, one of the things we've talked about too is that your point is absolutely correct, that AIs do better if they're constrained in what they're looking at and they're constrained in the problem they're given. They're kind of like humans, right? If you give them too much to think about at once, stuff gets lost and forgotten and whatever. So if you can constrain the code base, they're going to do better.

But on the flip side, for example, we had three JavaScript separate services, separate repos, but they were sort of drifting in different directions for no good reason. And so we merged those back together and then the AI has started to pick up good practices from one and apply it to the others.

So it can occasionally be useful with AI to have stuff in, I guess this is more a mono repo than a mono service, but still a similar idea of pulling everything back together. So I don't know that we have the perfect answer yet because your point is still correct, but I think we're still trying to figure out when is it better to pull things together versus split them apart and what are the advantages to each side?

Michael Stiefel: Well, one thing that occurred to me as I've thought about this problem, and anybody who is curious about this is thinking about this problem ... none of us have answers to it ... but I think about not only the creation of the code at the start, but when you start to get bug reports back, how do you alter the AI generated code?

So if you have a monolith or you have one repo or you have something large, it may be harder for the AI to make the micro changes or the larger changes that have to be made if you're dealing with a monolith rather than a microservice. Because I had someone on the podcast who we talked about this and his whole idea was you have the AI generate the microservice, and when you get a bug report in, you just regenerate the microservice from scratch because you can do that with an AI much more easily than you can with a human.

So I don't know how you feel about that. It's not so much the initial creation, but it's when you loop back the bug report or the changes from the field that the SREs are bringing in or the customers reported, that the advantage of microservices really comes to the fore.

Joy Ebertz: I haven't actually dabbled in anything that extreme. I have heard other people talk about it as well. And I'm really fascinated by this concept of just having AI completely regenerate something because to your point, it is much, much faster to build the entire thing than it used to be. I do think the thing we're missing is good testing. I think in order to do that, you have to have all of your use cases very well-defined in tests or in some form. As you rebuild a thing, you need to make sure it still meets all of the needs that you have, which is I think a limiting factor for a number of teams out there at the moment.

The Importance of Requirements and Testing [09:29]

Michael Stiefel: Well, that raises the other question, and I've been in this business long enough. I mean, I remember, and it's curious when I think about this, because I remember the arguments over whether compilers or hand-coded assembly code was better or not. This is the software business, all things old are new again. But in those days, there was a dream, and I'm thinking about the 1980s, early 1990s, that we would have these requirement definition languages that would remove the ambiguity.

See, this is the problem. English is wonderful or anything ... I'm picking English out, but it's true of all languages. So I'm just using English because that's the language I know best. I'm not trying to prejudice against some other language or some other culture, but language is purposely ambiguous because it's much better very often diplomatically or culturally just to be slightly ambiguous than precise.

Computers, on the other hand, are stupid. I mean, even at some level, they're dumb. And even the AI today, maybe 50 years from now, 20 years from now, they'll be smarter than we are, but not where we are right now and not for the foreseeable future. So the question is, if you're going to have those tests, A, how are you going to describe them precisely? Because if the AI is generating the tests, presumably a separate AI is going to generate the test, but if you have the tests, how are you going to describe them precisely enough?

Because let's say you're doing TDD and you want to write your test first, and it's one thing for me to write a test and looking through requirements, document a conversation with the customer or the program manager, however it came about, and write a test, but for the AI to take that written statement, do we need a language to do this? Is this something that still should be done by humans if the AI is generating the code? I mean, you see what I'm struggling with, and if you have any insights into that.

Joy Ebertz: I don't know that I have great insights, but when I first started playing with AI, one of the first things one of my teammates said was like, "Look, it's great. It generates the code and then it fixes all the tests it broke". And I was like, "Wait a minute, it's just doing whatever it wants".

Michael Stiefel: It could write it as assert true, and then the test passes.

Joy Ebertz: Yes, exactly. And I also have had cases where I'm like, "Fix this test", and the AI was like, "Okay, I'll delete the test". And I'm like, "Well, technically we don't have broken tests now, but not what I meant". So I think we do need to figure that out.

I mean, I think you can still have AI generate tests, but I think you need to make sure that it's separate or there's clear commands that as a part of this rewrite, you don't touch any of the tests or much clearer on that side than we are right now, in general at least. I know our code base, we now have in our agent files things like "Don't just delete tests", and things like that.

Michael Stiefel: I mean, this is one of the places where you've talked about avoiding perfectionism, but here's almost the place where you have to be perfect or aim for perfectionism. Especially on the test then, because if you're going to rely on the AI to generate the code, all right, there regenerates slop, okay, that will come out in the process. But it's really the tests, and in this world, the way I think about it, the tests become even more important than they were.

Joy Ebertz: Yes, it's interesting because I guess, and this is a shift in thinking in general, is, previously you would have an old system and even if there were small bugs or it was really annoying to maintain, sometimes it was worth just not touching because you didn't know what the requirements were exactly. Nobody in the company remembers anymore what all the requirements are. So it's easier to just leave it and not touch it, or touch it as little as possible. And it's still going to mostly work. But with this new model of maybe we regenerate huge chunks of it regularly, you need to know what it's supposed to do and you need to somehow document that or something in a way that we've been traditionally very lazy about.

In fact, I heard this a couple days ago. It was like, "We are not writing enough documentation. It's not clear what our stuff does". Because nobody does; that's just not something that happens.

Michael Stiefel: Well, let me tell you, I've been doing this since around 1982, and we still in those days said we're not writing enough documentation or ... So I mean, this is a problem, especially as the speed of development increases.

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Michael Stiefel: This might actually turn out to be the gating factor. It's not the AI slop, whatever that means, but the fact that we cannot generate requirements well enough and we can't feed back what comes back to the field to those requirements fast enough.

Joy Ebertz: I think that's right because I've been hearing recently that code reviews and some of that is what's gating it right now, but I think that's an artificial gate because I think as the tests improve and some of that stuff, we're going to stop relying on code reviews. Because code reviews are never great to begin with, if I'm being honest.

Michael Stiefel: I've done them, so I know exactly where you're coming from.

Joy Ebertz: Yes. Sometimes they catch stuff, but a lot of times they don't catch a lot of the things. And as you're getting inundated with more and more code reviews, none of us signed up to just code review all day. None of us like that. We're just getting sloppy at the code reviews too. So I think they have to go away and we have to find a way for them to go away.

So once you get rid of that, I think it gets replaced with tests and requirements and some of the stuff you're talking about, and I think it comes back more to how fast can we think through the problems and define the behaviors we want to see and how well can we define the system as a whole?

Michael Stiefel: Because if you remember the extreme TDD people went and said they actually define the system as they wrote the tests because the tests were almost the requirement. I mean, I never believed in that extreme to begin with. That's too much ceremony. You weren't done until the tests were done, but the idea is that you'd evolve the tests and that would tell you what the requirements are, and that's clearly not going to work here in this world.

Human Technological Knowledge Disappears [16:03]

Thinking about what we've moved the conversation to, there's still going to be some problems that humans are going to have to investigate. I think especially some of the security problems, some of the interface with third parties, because if we're using third party libraries or third party services, they're not going to be very often well-defined. So how the hell are you going to tell the AI what to be well-defined? So in those scenarios or the tough bugs or whatever it is, we're going to have to read the AI-generated code.

However, if the AI start to, or the agents or whatever, we're obviously being sloppy about what we mean by the term AI here, but I think in the ambiguity of the conversation, the event of being humans, talking to humans-

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Michael Stiefel: ... we understand. The question becomes if the AI writes the software, does it start to write the software for the machine and other AIs and not human consumption? Because I remember that's part of the debate that happened with the compilers and the machine language that you would have at some point, until the compilers got really good. I mean, now no one really worries about that kind of thing. Although I'm old enough to remember when we found bugs in compilers or we found bugs because the compiler switches weren't right.

I mean, this is not to show you, I don't know if anybody in this generation would understand this, but I remember one time I was called in as a consultant to solve a problem where all of a sudden these huge builds stopped working. And what took me a little while, I had to go down the call stack and watch the calls as one library called another, and what I finally deduced was at one interface point, the two libraries are compiled with different compiler switches for which word boundaries the commands were reliant on. So in the call stack, the argument transfer didn't work, and that's why the thing was blowing up. Now, most developers today would not be able to handle that problem because it's just assumed away. In other words, the abstractions have been piled up and the virtual machines have been piled up, and the only reason why I could figure it out is because I was old enough to remember the days when you worried about things like that.

So my fear is in this transition period, because we're going faster ... See, in those days we didn't go fast, so there was time for people like me to adapt to new technology and keep up and still retain the old knowledge. My fear is if we go so fast, this old knowledge will be rapidly forgotten.

Training Junior Engineers to User AI Effectively [18:54]

Joy Ebertz: I think it's related to that, but one of the things I worry about is we're not effectively teaching the next generation. Because I know senior engineers right now, I suspect we just know what to ask the AI a little bit better and we frame it in terms of like, "I want to use this database and kind of roughly structure it like this". You give it pretty specific instructions with the architecture kind of already built in and then have it do the thing. But I've seen some fairly junior engineers who come in and just give it very generic things and you end up with like spaghetti code doing who knows what, that kind of does the thing but not great. And as a senior engineer, I don't know how to necessarily train them or which pieces of what I'm telling the AI I need to train them to start doing.

It's this much harder to teach them this thing that I was never specifically taught. So we're not teaching them to use the AI effectively, but we're also not teaching them how to do it without the AI, which is kind of where I came from in order to be where I am today.

Michael Stiefel: So I'll put it even more bluntly, is the code that we're asking AIs to do with traditionally the code that the apprentice has learned on.

Joy Ebertz: There's some of that as well for sure.

Michael Stiefel: And this is a topic I've tried exploring on the podcast before and I would love to explore again, is how do we train the next generation of engineers? Because I think there's a serious problem here and we're moving too fast. Because for example, I had this actual conversation at lunch with a friend of mine. Do you tell people to study computer science as an undergraduate?

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Michael Stiefel: Or do you tell them, and I had this conversation with many people who are senior engineers and have children going into college and what advice do they give them? There's more to it than just telling the AI what to do.

Joy Ebertz: Yes. I honestly don't know if I would tell somebody to go into CS today. Most companies at the moment are just not hiring junior engineers too, which also feels shortsighted. At some point everybody's going to retire out of the workforce and who are they going to have left?

Michael Stiefel: Where are all the COBOL programmers?

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Michael Stiefel: Somebody once said to me, I mean we were having a discussion, some companies are still hiring junior engineers because they're cheaper than all the tokens they need to produce the code. But at some point that won't be the case. So neither of us have an answer to this question. And I have a feeling, like most things in our discipline, in fact, most things we do with human beings, they don't learn until there's a crash or failure of some sort. In other words, I don't know if this is an evolutionary defect that we're so short-term-minded, but we don't get the next thing done without thinking ... This is what you were talking about before about the architect. As an architect, you should be thinking about the long-term and that the long-term is where we're going to get the developers from.

Joy Ebertz: Exactly.

Michael Stiefel: I mean, I've had people suggest to me maybe you pair-program with the AI or you give the junior developers to ask them to debug certain problems, but these seem to be ad hoc solutions. This is something that somebody's going to have to figure out. And neither you nor I seem to have the answer to ... Ah, I'm not surprised, but it's going to have to emerge. I think what's going to happen is people are going to just have to bite the bullet and not assign certain problems to AI, to just train the junior developers.

Joy Ebertz: Yes. But it's interesting, especially with capitalism, what company is incentivized to do that? Very few of them are.

Michael Stiefel: Well, first of all, you have the same problem in other economic systems. It's just in capitalism it's more visible because you see the dynamic. If you have social systems that do bureaucratic long-term planning, you don't see it because the signals aren't there. But that's an interesting discussion we're going to have some other time.

To me, the advantage of capitalism has always been that the signals are obvious. The question is what you do about the signals. This is where you can argue about social policy and what's right and what's not. But if you hide the signals, it's like curing a fever with aspirin without asking yourself, "Well, why do we have a fever?"

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Michael Stiefel: Anyway, you would think the larger companies would have the time to look ahead because they have the market momentum. Unlike the smaller ventures who have to get a product to market to show, you think the larger companies would, where this would come from, but I don't see them doing this either or figuring this out.

Joy Ebertz: Yes. Which sort of ties back into my tech debt talk as well. The larger companies can afford to build things the right way and generally do things the right way for the long term. And to your point, I would hope that they would start to do this as well, but I haven't seen evidence of it quite yet, but I guess we're still fairly early.

Michael Stiefel: Well, I mean, I think we will see evidence of this quickly because if people start to move ahead quickly with AI. And all you need is one bad situation and everybody will now panic in the opposite direction. So we'll see what happens.

AI Coding and Hard Technical Problems [24:37]

One other question I was thinking about, I was thinking about talking to ... You've spent a lot of time dealing with authorization. And to me, I mean, everyone talks about authentication, but to me in my experience, authorization is a much harder problem because it's fine-grained. I mean, I once had a situation where I had a client where certain columns and reports could only be read by certain people. Authorization can get down to a really, really gnarly problem in a way that authentication seems relatively ... "Okay, just make sure the token flows".

Authentication and Authorization

Joy Ebertz: Yes. Authentication is very complex, but it's also a pretty well-defined problem and people understand it fairly well. Authorization, to your point, the simple case is pretty easy, but then you can very quickly add many, many rules, many, many special cases on top of that. And it gets very, very complex very quickly.

Michael Stiefel: Do you think artificial intelligence could help with this?

Joy Ebertz: That's a great question. I mean, it helps with a lot of things, so I don't want to say no. But then on the flip side, there's also the case or what we were talking about originally where it doesn't do well with large problems either, large complex systems either. So I don't know.

Michael Stiefel: Well, that's fair. I mean, that's a lot more honest than an LLM will be, which would never say I don't know.

Joy Ebertz: Actually, I have had it a couple times be like, "Oh, I think I'm going in circles here". But, anyway.

Michael Stiefel: I mean, not to get too far afield, but I've had that problem. Let's say you're using RAG and it can't find in your sources that you gave it from the RAG an answer. It will go back and instead of saying, "I don't know", it'll go back into its training data and come up with an answer.

Joy Ebertz: Yes. One of my least favorite coworkers tended to do that too. If he didn't know something, he would make something up, and so you couldn't trust anything out of his mouth.

Michael Stiefel: Well! So this would be someplace where I think ... I haven't dealt with authorization problems in a long time, but I figured you having your experience and also experience with AI might be able to have some insight into that problem, but as you say, it can be a global problem which AI has problems with.

Joy Ebertz: Yes. I think part of why people struggle with authorization is it starts simple. Like I said, any new company, it starts very simple. So they just build something simple. They don't use a vendor or anything. Makes sense. And then they slowly tack on more and more and more rules until it's this giant monstrosity that nobody really understands. And from what I've seen from there, is the best path forward is usually to break that up and try to put these into more well-constrained rules and problems and kind of separate the domains a little bit. And I think at that point, sure, an AI can deal with that because it's like the constrained problems again, but whether it would be good at breaking it up in the first place, maybe. I guess I haven't tried it, but I would also be a little scared because this is authorization we're talking about.

Michael Stiefel: Right, right. I mean, this might be something you would try in some sandbox. I would be curious to know.

Joy Ebertz: Now I'm curious. Yes.

Michael Stiefel: Because I mean, not that I read the entire literature, but I have not seen anybody really talk about this. Because a lot of talk has been about AI coding, microservices, monoliths, the slop, testing, a lot of the things that we've talked about, but some of these classic architectural problems like authorization ... I mean, it doesn't help, of course, the authorization technologies are sometimes opaque in themselves.

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Michael Stiefel: It might be interesting, I haven't tried this, to query an LLM on trying to see if they understand RBAC or any of these technologies because I find humans have problems with them. But to think about these things like scalability or security in general or user experience, and again, I mean end-to-end user experience. You would think the AIs have anything to contribute to this?

Joy Ebertz: You're naming all of the places where I think humans are still the most important. Yes. It's like places where you really care about performance, places where you really care about security, end-to-end user experience. Yes, I've tried to ask an AI like, "Center this on the screen", and it failed like seven times in a row, so.

Middle Tier Architecture and Orchestration [29:21]

Michael Stiefel: Do you think there's a place for AI in the middle tier? In other words, one architecture I've seen, and I've seen it talked about in multiple places, is the orchestrator pattern, where you have, let's say the AI generates the microservices. So the question is who does the orchestration? Because to me, the way I naively like to think about software, or architecture, this is sort of like the meal planning model of software. You have the microservices or the fundamental services, the basic services are sort of the ingredients. The front end is sort of the final meal that the user sees. But the real hard stuff happens in the middle tier; you take the basic ingredients and you put together, in some sense, the business is in the middle tier. The UI is just for the humans.

So if you're orchestrating these things, let's say the AI is writing the microservices and we've solved the problems that we've talked about before. Do you think it's reasonable that AIs either now or in the foreseeable future be able to orchestrate these things? If you give it a defined business problem, maybe they could do the orchestration.

Joy Ebertz: It certainly seems plausible that we could get there. I'm unsure if we're there now. I guess we keep coming back to sort of the same point of it doesn't do well with large things necessarily, so if you can constrain that business problem enough, I could imagine it doing okay. But is it worth it is another question too.

Michael Stiefel: Yes. But what you're also saying is, to abuse a phrase from another place, there's a chasm to be crossed. So in other words, maybe early on, the AI could do the orchestration when your problem is simple, but as you get more customers and things get more complicated, you cross a chasm where the AI can't do it, but then you're sort of left with, A, people who don't know how to do the orchestration, and then whatever slop or mess or good stuff that the AI created to begin with and you may not be able to bridge that gap.

Joy Ebertz: Yes. It's an interesting time right now because we still have mostly code that was written by humans and we're still building mostly on that, so things are pretty easy, but as we move more to the point where almost all the code has been written by AI, I think things will start or will continue to shift. It'll shift through that and it'll be, to your point, even harder sometimes to do things.

What Does "We Are Coding WIth AI" Really Mean? [32:06]

Michael Stiefel: I mean, I was at Google Next about two weeks ago and one of the statements that got made, I think it was in one of the keynotes or whatever, that 75% of the code written at Google is written by AI in one way or another. Now, I didn't get a chance to query the person who made that statement or investigate that statement. Are they including configuration? I mean, what is that 75%? Does that include the tooling that people use, that it's okay if it's a little sloppy because people using it on the outside doesn't see it? Is it really organizing configuration files? I don't know what's in that 75%, but that is an impressive figure if it's true.

Or it just states that most of the code that we write is not that important. And what I mean is I've seen figures before that something like 80% of the code in a system is error checking, user input, just presenting things to humans, and it's not the core functionality. So maybe all they're doing is automating the "easy stuff", which is 75% for the coding task anyway. So I'm really curious to know what that 75% represents.

Joy Ebertz: I'm curious now too, because if you had asked me how much we're doing, I would say it's closer to a hundred. But for example, I'm working on an internal tool and the front end for that, I am a hundred percent vibe coding. I am barely looking at what code it spits out. I test it manually and I'm like, okay, this thing works, but it's an internal tool. If it's a little broken, nobody cares. But when I'm playing with our backend systems, I'm much more careful about, okay, telling the AI exactly how it needs to be written and then going through and checking that code. Sure, the code is still written by the AI, but I would say I'm validating basically every step of that.

And so even if you say all of the code was written by AI, those two are very different statements depending on which end of that spectrum you're on.

Michael Stiefel: Right. And it's almost, if I can be a little sardonic, if it's almost in that second case, you're almost using the AI as a sophisticated auto complete.

Joy Ebertz: Like a pair programmer that you're working with.

Michael Stiefel: Yes, yes.

Joy Ebertz: It's paid to double check you and vice versa.

Michael Stiefel: So what we're saying is when people say that the code was written by AI, we really have to qualify what kind of code we're talking about and how much human supervision and cooperation was there. For example, in the scenario you presented, you are the more senior of the pair and the other person's actually typing, but you are looking over their shoulder and saying, "This is not right", or, "Maybe you should do it this way".

Joy Ebertz: Yes, exactly.

Michael Stiefel: So going forward, we really have to be very careful when we present to people and say, "This was code written by an AI", what we actually mean by that.

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Michael Stiefel: I'm very fascinated by this conversation because it's getting me to think about what do we really mean when we say AI is helping us and what the limits to it are and how we're really going to figure this out?

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Constraints Are Your Friend [35:21]

Michael Stiefel: Does this flexibility that AI gives you become a nightmare? Because one of the things that I've seen in my career is that constraints always help you.

Joy Ebertz: Yes.

Michael Stiefel: In other words, because they take a huge ... I mean, you must have seen this when you do domain-driven design. In other words, the constraints are actually what pushes the conversation forward. You don't get to event storming until you have a relatively well-defined problem and it's the constraints that help you.

Joy Ebertz: Yes, I was actually, this is a totally different scenario, but I was in a planning meeting recently and we're just going in circles, but a lot of it, to your point, is just that it wasn't clear what the constraints were. People were asking, is something along these lines vaguely possible? Well, yes, but what exactly is that going to look like? And there were five different answers and it wasn't clear which one you pick because it wasn't clear what we were trying to solve for or what the real problems were or the constraints, to your point. So, yes.

Understanding Complexity and Assumptions [36:21]

Michael Stiefel: Yes. And what also that raises the question, and I've seen this over and over again, I presume you have too, is that non-technical people do not understand the complexity. Because how many times in your career someone has come to you and said, "Oh, this should be an easy change". But what the change they're asking for contradicts the fundamental assumptions you've made in the system. So it's really a big change. And at the same time, people come to you and say, "I know this is going to be horrible to change and it's going to give you a lot of work". And you realize, "Oh, I just change an if statement and it's done".

And I just wonder in the world of, again, AI coding, how are we going to answer those questions? How are you going to estimate the complexity of doing something? Or how long is this going to take both in just compute time to get it done and to correcting the AI? Because you don't know what the ... This is the other, you don't know what assumptions the AI has made in creating the code.

Joy Ebertz: Yes. We usually do a plan first and then have it code. My favorite question to ask it when it finishes the plan is what assumptions have you made? And then I go through those assumptions and do something one way or the other. But it's fascinating to see what it tells me because sometimes it's not a lot. And sometimes there's these huge assumptions, I'm like, "I'm glad I asked. That is totally wrong".

Michael Stiefel: This sounds like a real talk for a conference or a paper to be written about what it really means to code with AI. I mean, you've really come up with some interesting things based on experience that I don't think people appreciate. There's a lot of experience that you've had and a lot of experience you've put forward that I think is worth an article or a talk.

Joy Ebertz: I think what's interesting about this at the moment too is that we're all sort of in our own little bubbles learning these things on our own, and we don't necessarily have a lot of insight into how even our coworkers are using AI. I suspect some of them are doing some things better than I am and some things worse.

Michael Stiefel: Well, that says that maybe the next QCon, there should be a conference track on how are we actually using this AI thing?

Joy Ebertz: Yes, but on a personal level even, not like the large scale stuff, but just how exactly are you talking to the AI? What questions are you asking? What are you prompting it?

The Architect's Questionnaire [38:50]

Michael Stiefel: Maybe this is a meetup or a non-conference or something, because these are all questions that people don't really have answers to, and I think they're all important questions. So I've been very fascinated by this conversation, and I would like to now shift into what I like to call the more humane part of the podcast where I get to ask my architect's questionnaire and it's always interesting to me because no matter how many times I ask this, I always get some very interesting ideas from people and very different perspectives on what it means to be an architect. So what is your favorite part of being an architect?

Joy Ebertz: I'm sort of a big picture person anyway, and so it allows me to use that in a way that solves problems. I guess ultimately I really like solving problems, and so it's like the intersection of how I think anyway and the problem solving, which I find fun and exciting.

Michael Stiefel: What is your least favorite part of being an architect?

Joy Ebertz: Some of the problems you encounter are these long event horizon things that you're trying to affect and change, and it can be very frustrating to get them prioritized and continue to get them prioritized and continue to decide if they're even worth getting prioritized this next time. And maybe it never comes to anything, and then did you make the right decision originally? You know what I mean? This long cascade of how do you get things to happen or roll in the direction that you're hoping that they roll?

Michael Stiefel: Is there anything creatively, spiritually, or emotionally intriguing about architecture, being an architect?

Joy Ebertz: To my point of liking to solve problems, I feel like it's just more problems and more complexity and you're thinking about more things. So I don't know, it's just exciting problem solving.

Michael Stiefel: What turns you off about architecture or being an architect?

Joy Ebertz: I think there's still that image of the ivory tower architect floating around, which I've never liked. I hope I never turn into. I hope I'm not. But trying to figure out how to bridge that gap of having enough level above that you can see the entire picture and that you can figure out how to pull everything in, but still have enough grounding in the team that you're working with so that they trust you and all that kind of stuff. And how do you balance that? But I'm constantly trying to figure out how to balance that in a reasonable way.

Michael Stiefel: Do you have any favorite technologies?

Joy Ebertz: Probably not.

Michael Stiefel: That's fair.

Joy Ebertz: I don't know. I've generally viewed technologies as just tools to help me solve the problems, and it's the problems that I find interesting more so than the technologies. A lot of technologies are good in some scenarios and absolutely terrible in others. So it's matching the technology for the problem you have at hand.

Michael Stiefel: What about architecture do you love?

Joy Ebertz: When things go well, it's pretty exciting because you can really see how you've made something simpler, you've made something cleaner, you've enabled something to last longer.

Michael Stiefel: What about architecture do you hate?

Joy Ebertz: A lot of times that doesn't happen. Just honestly, I kind of mentioned this before too, but a lot of times these are long horizon things and you start to question whether this was even the right choice to begin with. And sometimes you change your mind and that's the best decision at the time. And yes, a lot of times these projects don't necessarily finish or don't get as far as you want them to. In fact, I've come to the side that most monoliths splitting into microservices projects, you don't actually expect it to finish. You expect it to get about 75% of the way there, and then that is actually success, but it's hard to see it that way sometimes.

Michael Stiefel: What profession other than being an architect would you like to attempt?

Joy Ebertz: I mean, most things in software are pretty fun, but I assume we're taking that off the table entirely. And somebody told me recently this would be terrible, so now I'm questioning, but I've always sort of wanted to be like a mail carrier because you get to walk around and do your own thing, and I don't know. Anyway, random thought, but totally unreal and good.

Michael Stiefel: Do you ever see yourself not being an architect anymore?

Joy Ebertz: I doubt it because I really like software. I really like solving problems. At the moment, I would say I'm probably a little bit, if you're talking like Will Larson's archetypes, I'm probably a little bit closer to the Right Hand than the Architect, but it doesn't mean that I stop thinking like an architect. Part of me is still an architect, even if it's only a small part at the moment. And I think that's going to generally be true. It's hard to get rid of that entirely.

Michael Stiefel: When a project is done, what do you like to hear from your clients or your team?

Joy Ebertz: Feedback. Any feedback, honestly. I think with these long-term projects I'm talking about, it's often hard to get feedback. And that leads to the ivory tower thing of you don't really know the outcomes, good or bad. And so getting those outcomes, even if it's bad, I would rather know it so I can learn from it.

Michael Stiefel: Well, thank you very much. I found this quite fascinating. I hope you enjoyed it as well, and thank you very much for being on the podcast.

Joy Ebertz: Yes, thank you for having me. This was fun.

entries.title: Presentation: You Can't Trust Your AI Bill. And Neither Can I
entries.summary: Erik Peterson discusses why AI spend is eclipsing cloud bills, triggering a major software engineering cost crisis. He explains tokenmaxxing, unit economics, forced developer promotions, and why fully autonomous AI will write, deploy, and govern code by 2028. By Erik Peterson
entries.content:
Transcript

Erik Peterson: I'm going to talk a little bit about the bill. There was a lot of conversation about all the great things that we're building. I think we really have gotten to a place where we're building an enormous amount of great things, but the bill comes due at some point. I wanted to share some of the things that I've been seeing, my company's been seeing, and make some wild-ass guesses about where I think it's all going. You all can hold me accountable to that. I can tell you, quite frankly, that it's a mess. Who am I? I'm Erik Peterson. I'm the CTO and founder of the company CloudZero. I started the company here in Boston in 2016. Coming up in August, almost on 10 years. It's been a wild and crazy ride over the last 10 years. Nobody could have predicted what's going on right now, or maybe somebody did. I'm sure somebody did. CloudZero is the financial control plane for cloud and AI. I'll share some of the data. Six months ago, we noticed something interesting happening in the bill.

Rise of AI

We are here. Really, we are here. This is what is happening. It is an amazing time that we can live in that if I want a money-flaming meteor and pounding it into the earth, I can just have whatever I want to create in front of me. How much did that cost to generate? I'm going to say this a few times today. I used to say every engineering decision is a buying decision. We are now in a world where every decision is a buying decision. I need to do some research, I'm going to go to Perplexity. I'm going to write some code, I'm going to go to Claude. I'm going to build some images, maybe I'll go to ChatGPT. Before I send that email, before I finish that thought, I am putting that information probably through some LLM somewhere. That costs money. Somehow, we've gotten ourselves in a situation where every thought we have is now monetized.

It sounds a little dystopian. Maybe it's the evolution of the human race. I certainly hope so. We are here. It costs money. The bill comes due. The bill is a little crazy. We have amazing statements like this being made. How many people saw this? Think about that. Take whatever your salary is, and if you don't spend half of that salary by the end of the year, Jensen doesn't think you're a great engineer. He's going to lose his mind. I think this may have kicked off, or maybe it was right in the heart of the tokenmaxxing universe. Tokenmaxxing, what is that rot upon the world? This is single-handedly probably the most expensive vanity metric in the history of IT. It's really hard to estimate exactly what that is. It's somewhere on the order of $5 billion to $15 billion. How many people had a boss or a manager or a CEO who was looking at the AI leaderboard — they're calling it a leaderboard — to figure out who in their organization was doing what they hoped they were doing with AI.

Did they know? No. They knew for a fact that if you weren't spending money, something must have been wrong. This is the craziest thing ever. Here we are. This term, I think, was invented back in March. It was declared over in May. I think it's still going. I think we're still living this. What has happened over the past couple months is pretty indicative of what's to come.

I think AI is coming for your jobs, too. If that meteor wasn't scary enough. Last year, I would say this definitively is not true. I was wrong. Last year, I would have said, you're not going to lose your job to AI. You're going to lose your job to somebody using AI. I actually think what's happening is we are getting a promotion. It's a forced promotion. We're going to have to accept it and change. Nothing drives this point home for me more than actually a story from my past. One of my first jobs in IT where I was working at a computer support job and had a couple of nice ladies walk into my office. They said, we used to work in this office and then you people with your computers showed up. We were six of us on typewriters. Typewriters had a real feel to them, a computer, soulless.

A couple weeks later, my head of HR asked me for a GitHub account. What? I don't know. Claude told me I needed a GitHub account in order to do this thing. I was like, do you know what GitHub is? She's like, I don't know what GitHub is, but it said that I needed it and it said that I should ask my IT person, and you're the technology. My observation was everybody in the company became a developer, a very junior developer, in that moment. The CEO was like, this is awesome, everybody is doing stuff. The CTO brain was like, ok, I think we're getting better. Everything blew up.
