entries.title: React 19.3: Adds a browser() API, Giving Client-Only Rendering a First-Class Name
entries.summary: React 19.3 was released on September 9, introducing several features including the react-dom browser() API. This API allows components to opt out of server-side rendering, addressing issues with components that rely on client-specific data. It provides a cleaner solution for managing hydration mismatches and supports conditional data fetching, enhancing flexibility for developers. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
React 19.3 shipped on npm on September 9, and alongside stable View Transitions and Fragment Refs it slips in a smaller but widely welcomed addition, a react-dom browser() API that lets a component formally opt out of server-side rendering. Aurora Scharff, who shared the docs, announced that the reference is now live and available in the Canary channel, where you pass the value to 

use()
and the component suspends on the server.

The problem it targets is familiar to anyone doing SSR. Components that read 

localStorage
, 
window
, or the device timezone cannot produce meaningful HTML on the server, and the existing workarounds were awkward. Developers either flipped a mounted flag inside an effect or guarded rendering with 
typeof window !== 'undefined'
, a pattern that causes hydration mismatches the moment the server and first client render disagree.

The new API replaces both:

import { use } from 'react';
import { browser } from 'react-dom';
function LocalTime() {
 use(browser());
 return 
{new Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone}
;
}

During server rendering, 

use(browser())
stops the component and leaves the nearest Suspense boundary's fallback in the HTML. In the browser it returns 
undefined
, so the component renders as normal after hydration. It must be called from a Client Component and sit inside a Suspense boundary, or the server render fails. Because 
use()
can live behind a condition, a component can defer only when it has to, for example a data hook that renders on the server when a loader supplies 
initialData
and opts out otherwise. React also adds an 
onBrowserBailout
callback and an optional reason argument so teams can report exactly where server rendering was skipped.

The change first landed as a React core PR that This Week in React described as "eliminating hacky server error-suppression workarounds". In the docs issue tracking the feature, one contributor wrote they were "very excited about the 

browser()
api because it solves the client-only component problem in a much cleaner way than the previous ways". Writing about the release, one developer called the conditional data-fetching version "the cleanest solution to the 'should this fetch on the server or not' question I've seen".

The approach also narrows the gap with framework-specific escape hatches. Next.js users have long reached for 

dynamic(() => import('./C'), { ssr: false })
via next/dynamic, and Astro exposes a client:only directive, but both are tied to their bundlers. 
browser()
moves the capability into React itself, so it works with any SSR setup rather than a single framework.

Upgrading is a standard bump to 

react@19.3
and 
react-dom@19.3
, following the React 19 upgrade guide, though the use reference still flags 
browser()
as Canary only, so confirm your release channel before depending on it in production.

React is an open-source JavaScript library for building user interfaces, originally created at Facebook and now maintained by Meta together with a large community of contributors. It popularised a component-based model in which the UI is described as a function of state, and it underpins server-side and full-stack frameworks such as Next.js and Remix, as well as native apps through React Native. Since its first release in 2013 it has become one of the most widely used front-end tools, with recent versions leaning further into server rendering, Suspense, and the concurrent features that the 

browser()
API builds on.

entries.title: Java News Roundup: Grails 8, Open Liberty, GlassFish, Infinispan, LangChain4j, Spock
entries.summary: This week's Java roundup for October 5th, 2026, features news highlighting: OpenJDK JEPs Proposed to Target for JDK 28; Lazy Constants elevated to Candidate status; the GA releases of Apache Grails 8.0 and Open Liberty 20.0.0.10; point releases of TornadoVM, Infinispan, LangChain4j and Spock; and a maintenance release of GlassFish. By Michael Redlich
entries.content:
This week's Java roundup for October 5th, 2026, features news highlighting: OpenJDK JEPs Proposed to Target for JDK 28; Lazy Constants elevated to Candidate status; the GA releases of Apache Grails 8.0 and Open Liberty 20.0.0.10; point releases of TornadoVM, Infinispan, LangChain4j and Spock; and a maintenance release of GlassFish.

OpenJDK

JEP 546, Adaptive Heap Sizing for ZGC, has been elevated from Candidate to Proposed to Target for JDK 28. This JEP proposes to "enhance the Z Garbage Collector to adaptively adjust the size of the heap based on the resources available, the application's needs, and the needs of neighboring applications contending for the same resources." The review is expected to conclude on Wednesday, October 14, 2026.

JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been elevated from Candidate to Proposed to Target for JDK 28. This JEP proposes to "improve application startup and warmup by enhancing the Z Garbage Collector to acquire and prepare physical memory more swiftly and efficiently in response to application needs." The review is expected to conclude on Wednesday, October 14, 2026.

JEP 543, Structured Concurrency, has been elevated from Candidate to Proposed to Target for JDK 28. This JEP proposes to finalize this feature, without change, after seven rounds of preview, delivered in JDK 21 through the upcoming release of JDK 27, and two rounds of incubator delivered in JDK 19 and JDK 20. This feature simplifies concurrent programming by introducing structured concurrency to "treat groups of related tasks running in different threads as a single unit of work, thereby streamlining error handling and cancellation, improving reliability, and enhancing observability." The review is expected to conclude on Tuesday, October 13, 2026.

JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8389764 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of 

final
fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.

JDK 28

Build 19 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 18 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

GlassFish

The release of GlassFish 8.0.5 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: updates to the 

 class to include the ZipPayloadImpl
Header ID
 and 
Data Size
 values in the extra header as per the ZIP64 Extra Fields (JDK-8302483) specification; and improvements in deployment time for both large and small applications. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
    
Apache Grails

    
The release of Apache Grails 8.0.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for JDK 21 and Gradle 9.7 as minimal versions; all controllers are now REST resources that resolve a controller from the request as opposed to the mapping; and Grails Promises now run on top of the Spring Boot Task Executor. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

    
TornadoVM

    
The release of TornadoVM 7.2.0 and 7.1.0 provide notable changes such as: new methods, 
mmaLoadA()
 and 
mmaLoadB()
, added to the 
 class, that return 8-element and 4-element fragments, respectively, of the KernelContext
 class; and updates to the HalfFloat
, CUDACommandQueue
 and CUDAEvent
 classes such that they now accurately report the driver dispatch time for kernel launches and data transfers. Further details on these releases may be found in the release notes for CUDAHandlesversion 7.2.0 and version 7.1.0.
    
Open Liberty

    
The GA release of Open Liberty 26.0.0.10 delivers: bug fixes; support for JDK 27; and resolutions to seven CVEs affecting various Open Liberty features. Developers should note that, with G1 now the default GC in all environments, users running Open Liberty in a constrained environment may experience a different garbage collection behavior compared to earlier Java versions.

    
Infinispan

    
The release of Infinispan 16.3.0, codenamed Tripel Karmeliet for "robustness," ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a more efficient hash-based conflict detection and resolution when merging partitions; enhanced configuration as attributes are now persisted to survive restarts; and improved logging to reduce log noise. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

    
LangChain4j

    
The formal release (along with the thirty-second beta release) of LangChain4j 1.22.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new 
 class that implements the core BedrockBatchChatModel
 interface on the Bedrock batch inference API; and new BatchChatModel
 and OpenAiDecisionModel
 classes to support the OpenAI OpenAiOfficialDecisionModelDecisions API. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
    
Micronaut

    
The release of Micronaut Framework 5.2.2, based on Micronaut Core 5.2.15, delivers an update to Netty 4.2.19.Final featuring resolutions to 16 CVEs including HTTP request/response smuggling and unbounded resource consumption in the HTTP, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 codecs. There were also patch updates to modules: Micronaut Data and Micronaut Test Resources. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

    
Spock

    
The release of Spock 2.5.0 ships with bug fixes and new features such as: support for Groovy 6 and Spring Framework 7; improvements to the 
 class that now reports unsatisfied interactions for easier diagnosis of mismatched invocations; and support for local variables declared as TooManyInvocationsError
final
 in 
where:
 blocks. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes.

entries.title: GitLab 19.4 Adds Goal-Driven Agents and Tighter Cost Controls
entries.summary: GitLab has released version 19.4 of its DevSecOps platform, adding a goal-driven mode to GitLab Duo CLI, three hosted open-weight models, a larger set of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, and more detailed controls for AI spending. By Matt Saunders
entries.content:
GitLab has released version 19.4 of its DevSecOps platform, adding a goal-driven mode to GitLab Duo CLI, three hosted open-weight models, a larger set of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, and more detailed controls for AI spending. The release moves GitLab's agents beyond individual prompts and predefined flows, while keeping their actions within the permissions and approval rules already used by a project.

The new /goal command in GitLab Duo CLI, now in public beta, accepts an open-ended objective and continues working until it completes the task or reaches an iteration limit. One model implements the changes while a separate model checks progress against the stated goal. A developer can stop the run, change the goal, or redirect the agent. The work runs locally and retains the project's existing context and controls.

"This release takes agentic automation from something individual developers use to something an organization can scale at speed and under the controls already in place."

Manav Khurana, GitLab

GitLab's use of the word "verified" has a specific meaning here. The second model judges whether the result meets the natural-language goal; this is not formal verification of the code. The command can report work that it could not resolve, and the iteration limit prevents it from continuing indefinitely. Clear acceptance criteria therefore remain important, even though the developer no longer has to supervise every intermediate step.

GitLab Duo Agent Platform also gains support for the hosted open-weight models Kimi K3, MiniMax M3 and GLM 5.3. GitLab says these provide up to four times as many calls per GitLab Credit as many comparable frontier models. Group owners can set a default model for a feature and restrict the models available to teams. This lets an organisation use a lower-cost model for routine work and reserve a more expensive model for tasks where it performs better. The announcement does not include model-by-model benchmark results or absolute per-call prices, so customers will still need to test the options against their own workloads.

"The platform running the automation is what governs which tools an agent can touch and attributes what it consumes."

Manav Khurana, GitLab

The expanded GitLab MCP server tools let agents in third-party clients trigger and inspect pipelines, open and review merge requests, update work items, browse repositories, and manage vulnerabilities. Read-only tools default to "Always Allow", while write and delete operations default to "Always Ask". Administrators can change those rules at group or project level. Most of the MCP tools are available on the Free, Premium and Ultimate tiers, although the vulnerability management tools require Ultimate.

This is part of a wider move to let coding agents act through MCP without granting unrestricted access. InfoQ reported in 2025 that Google's Agent Mode for Android Studio could use MCP to reach external tools. GitHub Copilot also supports MCP across its main interfaces, with enterprise policies for controlling access to servers. GitLab's approach applies a decision to each tool and places a human checkpoint in front of changes by default.

Cost controls matter more when agents run automatically rather than in response to an individual prompt. DevOps consultancy and GitLab partner ReleaseTEAM cautions that "the practical risk is automation", because a flow attached to every pipeline failure or new merge request could run hundreds of times a day. It recommends setting usage caps before connecting a flow to a high-volume trigger, then measuring consumption in a limited pilot.

The fourth main change concerns cost attribution. Credit usage exports now include a row for each billable event, with the user, project, session, flow type, credits and token counts. A new settings page lets owners set a default per-user cap and add individual overrides without using the GraphQL API. Developers can see their own consumption, while billing managers receive warnings when on-demand use reaches 50% or 80% of a monthly cap.

The release follows a series of changes to GitLab Duo during 2026. GitLab 19.2 put agents to work on dependency remediation and security reviews, with a person still responsible for approving changes. Earlier, versions 18.10 and 18.11 introduced flat-rate automated code reviews, free-tier access to the Duo Agent Platform, and monthly credit limits. Version 19.4 extends that approach to longer-running development tasks and gives administrators a closer view of the resulting costs.

GitLab 19.4 was released on 17 September 2026. The /goal command is available to Premium and Ultimate customers on GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated, and requires GitLab 19.3 or later with Duo CLI 9.17.0 or later. The command and expanded MCP tools remain in public beta, while the new credit usage visibility is generally available.

entries.title: Xcode 27.2 Introduces an Agent- and Merge-Friendly JSON Format for Project Configuration
entries.summary: Apple is introducing a new JSON-based format for Xcode project configuration files, replacing the traditional property-list-based format. Available in Xcode 27.2, the new format aims to improve readability, simplify maintenance, and make project configuration easier for AI coding agents to understand and modify. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
Apple is introducing a new JSON-based format for Xcode project configuration files, replacing the traditional property-list-based format. Available in Xcode 27.2, the new format aims to improve readability, simplify maintenance, and make project configuration easier for AI coding agents to understand and modify.

The open source JSON file format (

xcode-project-format
) makes verifying project configuration changes easier when committing the project configuration file to your source code repository because changes in the comparison view correspond to your actions in Xcode.

A major advantage of the new format is that it reduces the likelihood of merge conflicts by providing a more stable and predictable representation of project configuration. The JSON format also makes the project structure more accessible to automated development tools, including AI coding agents, simplifying the inspection and modification of project settings.

To help developers work with the new format, Apple has also released a Swift package for encoding and decoding the new format. For example, this is how you list all targets defined in a project:

import XcodeProjectFormat


func listTargets(in projectURL: URL) throws {
    let projectData = try Data(contentsOf: projectURL)
    let project = try XCSchema.Project(jsonRepresentation: projectData)
    for target in project.targets {
        print(target.name)
    }
}

At the top-level, JSON schema defines not only targets but also the file tree, build configurations, build settings, and external dependencies. It also supports relationships between nodes in different subtrees. For example, a file specifies the build phases and targets it belongs to. Importantly, the formats avoid opaque identifiers wherever possible, favoring human-readable names and paths instead. Targets and build products are notable exceptions, as they use identifiers to support references from external files.

Commenting the announcement, senior iOS developer Nikita Dyachkov notes that

The issue of merging project files has been a long-standing problem since project files were introduced and was familiar to anyone who's worked in an iOS development team with more than one developer.

In the same thread, senior iOS engineer Khushal Jhalani described the new, more readable format as a "huge quality-of-life improvement". Others echoed the sentiment that the change was long overdue, with senior iOS developer Moumita China remarking that it could have saved "years of merge conflicts".

Existing projects can be migrated easily, as the new format changes only how the project is represented on disk, not its underlying model. Converting a project replaces the traditional 

project.pbxproj
file with 
project.xcproj
. Before migrating, however, ensure that any tools you are using, including fastlane, CocoaPods, Tuist, and others, support the new format.

entries.title: Context Language Models: Self-Managing Context to Improve Performance and Reduce Compute Costs
entries.summary: Researchers from Meta, MIT, and the University of Washington introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), a new approach that enables language models to manage and edit their own context rather than relying on predefined mechanisms for summarization, compression, and information retrieval, reporting substantial gains in both performance and computational efficiency. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
Researchers from Meta, MIT, and the University of Washington introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), a new approach that enables language models to manage and edit their own context rather than relying on predefined mechanisms for summarization, compression, and information retrieval, reporting substantial gains in both performance and computational efficiency.

The researchers implemented a mechanism that lets LLMs manage their own context by treating it as a file they can update without restrictions. This approach offers an alternative to conventional context-management strategies used to prevent context from growing indefinitely, such as compaction, offloading, and retrieval. Each technique has its own limitations. Summarization can discard critical details or introduce inaccuracies, compaction often uses a predefined set of rules, and external memory requires agents to decide what to bring back into the context.

A CLM can instead rewrite old messages, preserve important facts, remove irrelevant information, maintain progress notes, and learn its own context-management strategies. The researchers emphasize that LLMs can learn strategies that go beyond existing human-designed approaches, potentially surpassing "existing human priors".

By shifting context management from external harness control to intrinsic model behavior, CLMs naturally enable in-context learning and parametric learning for context management. We first show that users can steer context management simply by telling the agent their desired strategy. In addition, CLMs can evolve an in-context skill document that captures useful context-management procedures for future reuse.

New behaviors that CLM can learn include creating internal notes, removing irrelevant intermediate results while preserving useful ones, tracking unsuccessful experiments alongside ideas to explore further, and more.

The researchers explored three different approaches to context management. First, zero-shot context management, where the CLM received no specific training. Second, in-context learning, where the CLM was instructed using natural language on how to manage its context and refined its strategy through an iterative skill-optimization loop. Third, reinforcement learning, where the CLM learned context-management strategies using task success as the primary objective and computational efficiency as an additional optimization criterion.

The researchers evaluated CLMs across several benchmarks and reported substantial gains in both performance and computational efficiency. Zero-shot CLMs achieved:

11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus, 5% higher scores with 59% fewer FLOPs on 12-hour EdgeBench, and 65% greater improvement with the same compute on a 24-hour multi-repository agent-swarm task

CLMs using in-context learning improved accuracy on ContextBench tasks by up to 35.9 percentage points at lower compute. Finally, reinforcement learning improved Qwen3.5-9B performance on BrowseComp-Plus from 28.8% to 42.5%, a 47.6% relative improvement, while using 12% fewer FLOPs.

The researchers acknowledge several unresolved challenges. First, a CLM may discard important information that it cannot later retrieve. Second, allowing CLMs to edit their own context introduces new safety risks, as the editable context "can become another channel through which prompt injections or self-generated instructions persist across turns". Most importantly, greater control over context does not necessarily translate into better behavior, as models may still make poor decisions about what to retain, modify, or discard.

Commenting on the announcement on X.com, @Rennix7t warns that "the accuracy and computational power results in the paper come from specified tasks", while @omarsar0 describes the approach as an interesting research direction but expresses reservations about trusting a model to manage its context end-to-end, arguing that better solutions are still needed.

On Reddit, Combinatorilliance argues that CLMs are not yet production-ready, noting that rewriting the context invalidates the model cache and that the "caching trick [used by the researchers, EN] isn't ideal either and has some drawbacks that need to be taken into consideration".

entries.title: Foresight AI Brings Gremlin Agents to Reliability Engineering
entries.summary: Reliability management company Gremlin has announced the general availability of Foresight AI, an agentic product that analyses services for potential failures, recommends changes and reruns tests to check that a fix works. By Matt Saunders
entries.content:
Reliability management company Gremlin has announced the general availability of Foresight AI, an agentic product that analyses services for potential failures, recommends changes and reruns tests to check that a fix works. It is available as an add-on to the Gremlin platform. The platform allows teams to run planned experiments, control the blast radius of failures, and use automated testing to ensure that fixes remain effective over time. By using reliability scores, organizations can quantify their progress and prioritise their investments in resilience.

Foresight AI is intended to provide reliability checks without requiring every developer to become a distributed systems specialist. Gremlin positions the product as a response to faster AI-assisted software delivery, with Kolton Andrus, Gremlin's CEO and co-founder, arguing that more code is reaching production without close human review.

"The best incident is the one that never happens."

Kolton Andrus

The product divides work between four agent roles: an Analyst gathers service data and recommends tests, while a Tester schedules and runs them. An Operator interprets failed tests and proposes remediations. A technical program manager tracks test coverage, reliability risks and commitments across teams. The latter can produce weekly reports and send updates through Slack.

Foresight AI bases its recommendations on Gremlin's Failure Atlas. The company describes this as a proprietary record built from millions of fault-injection experiments conducted over more than ten years across tens of thousands of distributed systems. Gremlin says system data is not used to train a large language model. Instead, the agents use platform data and the Failure Atlas for decisions, with an LLM used for searching, summarising and explaining results.

The main technical distinction is the closed validation loop. When a test uncovers a weakness, the service proposes a change and then runs the original test again. Gremlin says Foresight AI will neither run a test nor apply a remediation without approval. This keeps an engineer responsible for changes while automating much of the analysis and repetition around them.

"An alert going quiet doesn't prove anything. A test that passes under load, in realistic conditions, does."

Kolton Andrus

The service also creates reports and dashboards from natural-language requests. These can include charts, tables, tabs and links, and are intended to show changes in reliability scores and the risks that teams have addressed. This tackles a familiar problem for reliability teams: avoided incidents do not produce the same visible evidence as outages.

In a separate article written for Gremlin, Intellyx analyst Jason English describes observability and AI SRE products as useful but largely reactive. He argues that they usually begin with telemetry from a problem that has already happened. Fault injection takes a different approach by creating controlled failure conditions before an incident and recording how a service responds.

English also cautions that a reliability programme cannot simply be installed as a software package. Sustained results still need shared ownership and accountability across engineering and management. This qualification matters because Foresight AI can coordinate tests and commitments, but an organisation must still decide which risks are acceptable and whether proposed changes should proceed. Intellyx discloses that Gremlin is its customer.

The release sits alongside other efforts to bring automated resilience checks into delivery pipelines, some of which have been covered recently by InfoQ. Google Cloud's chaos engineering guidance recommends realistic failure conditions, limited blast radii and continuous automation through CI/CD. Wix has also described using AI in CI/CD for log interpretation and remediation suggestions, while keeping deployment and critical infrastructure decisions under human control.

Those controls resemble the approval boundary in Foresight AI. They also differ from more autonomous models. Cloudflare's Agent Development Lifecycle proposal, for example, envisages agents managing more of testing, deployment and maintenance. Gremlin currently takes a supervised approach, using agents to propose tests and changes while requiring people to authorise them.

In a broader LinkedIn discussion about AI-based SRE automation, engineer Sandip Bhattacharya argued that organisations still need specialists to configure agents, assess their behaviour through metrics and adjust them as models and infrastructure change. This presents a useful test for Gremlin's supervised model: automation may reduce repetitive work, but it also creates a new system that reliability engineers must evaluate.

Mike Dauber, a general partner at Amplify Partners, compared Foresight AI to "a trainer who does the reps for you". His comment captures the product's emphasis on repeated testing, although the evidence presented so far comes from Gremlin and its beta programme. The company has not published comparative accuracy data, false-positive rates or detailed beta results.

Gremlin was founded by engineers with experience at Amazon and Netflix. Andrus previously worked on reliability at both companies, while Netflix's Chaos Monkey helped popularise automated failure injection. Foresight AI extends that approach from running experiments towards selecting tests, interpreting their results, proposing fixes and checking those fixes over time. This release follows a successful beta period where the technology demonstrated an ability to identify and address reliability risks before they cause incidents, and Gremlin Foresight AI is available for general use starting today.
